Let
\[
z=\frac1\lambda,\qquad q=\frac1\mu .
\]
Since \(0<\lambda<\mu<1\), we have \(z\ne q\). The answer is
\[
\boxed{
\frac{D_n(\lambda,\mu)}{D_n}
=
\frac{(\lambda\mu)^{2n}}{(q-z)^4}\,\mathcal C_n(z,q)
=
\frac{(\lambda\mu)^{2n+4}}{(\mu-\lambda)^4}\,
\mathcal C_n\!\left(\frac1\lambda,\frac1\mu\right)
}.
\]

Here \(\mathcal C_n\) is exactly the confluent Jacobi alternant from the problem statement.

**Proof.** Write the inner product
\[
\langle f,g\rangle=\int_0^1 f(x)g(x)w(x)\,dx.
\]
The Hankel determinant is the Gram determinant of \(1,x,\dots,x^{n-1}\), hence also of the monic orthogonal polynomials \(\pi_0,\dots,\pi_{n-1}\):
\[
D_n=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1} h_k,\qquad h_k=\langle \pi_k,\pi_k\rangle .
\]

First take four distinct complex numbers \(y_1,\dots,y_4\), and set
\[
R(x)=\prod_{\alpha=1}^4 (x-y_\alpha).
\]
Using Andreief’s determinant identity,
\[
\det\!\left[\int_0^1 x^{i+j}R(x)w(x)\,dx\right]_{i,j=0}^{n-1}
=
\frac1{n!}\int_{[0,1]^n}\Delta(x)^2\prod_{k=1}^n R(x_k)\prod_{k=1}^n w(x_k)\,dx_k,
\]
where \(\Delta(x)=\prod_{i<j}(x_j-x_i)\).

With
\[
\Delta(y)=\prod_{\alpha<\beta}(y_\beta-y_\alpha),
\]
one has
\[
\Delta(x)\prod_{k=1}^n\prod_{\alpha=1}^4(x_k-y_\alpha)
=
\frac{\Delta(x,y)}{\Delta(y)}
\]
because \(4n\) is even. Replacing monomials by the monic orthogonal basis \(\pi_0,\pi_1,\dots\), expand the determinant \(\Delta(x,y)\) along the four \(y\)-rows. Orthogonality kills every term except the one using columns \(n,n+1,n+2,n+3\) for the \(y\)-rows and columns \(0,\dots,n-1\) for the \(x\)-rows. Therefore
\[
\frac{\det\!\left[\int_0^1 x^{i+j}R(x)w(x)\,dx\right]_{i,j=0}^{n-1}}{D_n}
=
\frac{
\det[\pi_{n+j-1}(y_\alpha)]_{\alpha,j=1}^4
}{\Delta(y)}.
\]

Now let
\[
y_1=z,\qquad y_2\to z,\qquad y_3=q,\qquad y_4\to q.
\]
The numerator has the confluent limit
\[
(y_2-z)(y_4-q)\,\mathcal C_n(z,q)+o\bigl((y_2-z)(y_4-q)\bigr),
\]
while
\[
\Delta(y)
=
(y_2-z)(y_4-q)(q-z)^4+o\bigl((y_2-z)(y_4-q)\bigr).
\]
Hence
\[
\frac{\det\!\left[\int_0^1 x^{i+j}w(x)(x-z)^2(x-q)^2\,dx\right]_{i,j=0}^{n-1}}{D_n}
=
\frac{\mathcal C_n(z,q)}{(q-z)^4}.
\]

Finally,
\[
(1-\lambda x)^2(1-\mu x)^2
=
\lambda^2\mu^2(x-z)^2(x-q)^2.
\]
Multiplying the weight by the scalar \(\lambda^2\mu^2\) multiplies an \(n\times n\) Hankel determinant by \((\lambda^2\mu^2)^n\). Therefore
\[
\frac{D_n(\lambda,\mu)}{D_n}
=
(\lambda\mu)^{2n}\frac{\mathcal C_n(z,q)}{(q-z)^4}.
\]
Substituting \(z=1/\lambda\), \(q=1/\mu\) gives the stated formula.
